The Million Rand Pinky

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Road Accident Fund awarded R25 000 for an injured pinky finger, but the lawyers claimed R900 000

Summary:
In 2009 truck driver Welcome Ketsekele's truck collided with a concrete barrier injuring his pinky finger. In 2015, the RAF settled on an amount of R25 000 but his lawyers claimed R900 000 in damages and expenses. Judge Eberhard Bertelsmann challenged them to justify this claim before rubber-stamping the settlement. His ruling promises to set a precedent for future RAF claims.

Further information:
In 2010 UCT student Alison Law was run over while crossing the road. She suffered sever brain injuries and is now dependent on special care. In 2014 the RAF agreed to pay 100 % of her claim. The Western Cap0e High Court gave them 30 days to pay the R8 million, but this remains unpaid. The RAF have run out of money, partly due to the fact that lawyers like those representing Welcome Ketsekele, routinely claim at least R300 000 in costs. This leaves legitimate benefactors like Alison Law out of pocket and struggling to survive.

Press Release:


The R1-million Pinkie
When a truck driver injured his finger in an accident, his lawyers claimed nearly R1-million in damages from the Road Accident Fund. After a judge intervened to question the size of the claim, the driver was finally awarded only R25 000. Carte Blanche investigates the massive claims that have left the RAF broke and legitimate benefactors out of pocket and struggling to survive.


Script:


THE MILLION RAND PINKIE FINGER


V/O: In 2010 Alison Law had just matriculated and was studying to be a teacher. Throughout her teens she had been a talented dancer, becoming the national hip-hop champion. But at the age of 18 her supple, strong body would become a thing of the past when she was run over by a car in Main Road, Cape Town. Her father Jonathan showed us the scene.

Jonathan: We know that they were slightly on this side of the dotted white line. The vehicle heading south crossed over the line and hit Alison.

V/O: Alison was unconscious from the time of impact, and suffered a severe, diffuse head injury. After 5 months in a coma she had to learn to walk and talk again.

Alison: I was just 18, and I can’t really remember much of that life before the accident. All those memories have been completely wiped from my brain, so I cant don’t really have anything to compare myself to.

V/O: Now 23 Alison is still undergoing physiotherapy and speech therapy.

Alison: I still go through days where I realize that I can’t do what all my friends are doing. I can’t drive, I can’t study, I can’t hold down any job.

V/O; Alison’s lawyers put in a serious injury claim with the Road Accident Fund, and after almost 5 years she was awarded a multi-million rand settlement. But when it came time to pay out, the RAF didn’t have the money.

Jonathan: You get to the end of a process and there’s no money.

V/O: R1.50 of every litre of fuel sold is used to fund the RAF, that’s over R2 billion a month. But it’s not enough according to CEO Dr Eugene Watson.

Eugene: The problem is everybody has to wait. There just isn’t enough money to honour all payments at the same time.

V/O: So where is the money going? Last year the RAF paid R22 billion to accident victims, with R4.7 billion going on legal fees. But in a recent ruling at the Pretoria High Court Judge Bertelsmann has highlighted “the huge waste in legal fees and expenses”. It’s become known as the Ketsekele matter.

Ketsekele: I came from PE driving a truck. I was working for a company called Consolidated Freight

V/O: In January 2009 Sandi Ketsekele was travelling along the R21 near OR Tambo airport. Two taxis recklessly sped in front of his 34-ton truck and then suddenly slammed on brakes.

Ketsekele: Then I swerved to avoid hitting them.

V/O: The truck jack-knifed and collided with the barrier, much the same as this truck captured in footage on an American highway.

Ketsekele: As the truck hit the wall the front of the truck bent inwards and the steering wheel spun around and hit me here.

V/O; Ketsekele’s only injury was a fragmented fracture to his right hand pinkie finger.

John link: The million rand pinkie – it sounds ridiculous. But it’s the utter absurdity of the claim that appears to have presented Judge Bertelsmann with the ideal circumstances to highlight all that is wrong with the Road Accident Fund.

Judge: The injury suffered by the plaintiff – for such Mr Ketsekele was destined to become – could by no stretch of the imagination be described as serious.

V/O: A prosthesis replaced the joint of the little finger to the hand, and he spent 3 months recovering at home in Katlehong before returning to work. But a claim was lodged against the RAF by Ketsekele’s legal team that completely exaggerated his injuries. A medical doctor provided a report.

Chris: He didn’t describe it as an injury to the finger, he described it as a serious injury to the right hand, and identified two metacarpals as having been damaged. That was already a perversion of the truth.

V/O: Retired Judge Chris Greenland is a former Acting CEO of the Road Accident Fund. We gave him the Judgment to peruse.

Chris: This injury was escalated to be described as a very serious injury, which had already caused this man hospitalization, which was a blatant lie. He had never gone to hospital, except to have this injury attended to – it traumatized him, and that in future would cause him even emotional shock, pain and suffering.



V/O: His advocate, Willie Davel claimed that Ketsekele had suffered medical expenses of R100 000, loss of earnings of R50 000, future medical and hospital expenses were estimated at R100 000, and future loss of earnings of R250 000.

Judge: These sums added up to R550 000.

V/O: Even though Ketsekele was back at work after 3 months, Davel also claimed another R350 000 general damages for pain and suffering, making a grand total of 900 000.

Chris: That was the big lie that was perpetrated over 6 years and was finally presented, served up to the Judge and the Judge was asked to endorse it.

V/O: To support the claim, the attorneys also sent Ketsekele to a neuro-psychologist, an occupational therapist, an orthopaedic surgeon, an industrial psychologist and a general practitioner. But the experts all agreed that he didn’t suffer serious injury or impairment.

Judge: It is therefore clear that the only purpose these reports could ever serve was to churn the money machine for the attorneys and experts whose reports were obtained at R20 000 each.

Chris: The lawyers run the dispute, the argument, the quarrel – in this case they ran it for 6 years. And when they’ve got a nice pile of fees on both sides, at the door of the court – as happened here – they decide to settle.

V/O: Eventually on the day of the trial the legal representatives managed to reach a settlement. This is common in RAF matters according to the Chairperson of the Pretoria Bar Council.

Nana: You only have to go to the 6th floor of the High Court. You will mistake it for some stock exchange: the trading, the agreements on the 11th hour while the Judge is waiting to hear the matter.

V/O: Suddenly the figure of R900 000 went out the window and they agreed to pay Ketsekele just under R25 000 as well as the full costs of both legal teams and the medical experts. But Judge Bertelsmann had other ideas.

Judge: It is patently obvious that the lawyers involved in this matter, counsel and attorneys, confidently expected this forensic scam to be implemented without any problem, indicative of a practice that appears to be in vogue in RAF matters.

V/O: We asked Advocate Willie Davel for an interview, but he declined to comment, and was not at his chambers when we went to find him. The RAF”S lawyers and Advocate Sekgobela also declined to comment, saying their client had already done so.

Eugene: What would make us feel a lot better is if we had comfort early on our team actually put forward an offer, which was rejected. Then we can look at what our team did. The second thing we’ll look at is our legal representative to ascertain but why did they wait, so soon up until the moment of the trial to intervene?

John link: The cost of the RAF’s indifference in investigating these matters is astronomical. Judge Bertelsmann estimates that in one court term of 2015 alone the Fund wasted up to R150 million in legal fees.

V/O: What’s more – of all the civil matters heard in the Pretoria and Johannesburg High Courts this year, a staggering 90% were RAF matters.

Chris: There are many, many lawyers in that system who have never actually practiced law as I understand it, in that they’ve never represented anybody in court on anything meaningful. They’ve never advanced or defended human rights, but they are extremely wealthy simply by taking a cut out of claims of victims to the RAF.

V/O: But Judge Bertelsmann ruled that the only person who would get any money out of this case was Sandi Ketsekele.

Judge: The defendant is ordered to pay the sum of R24 941.70 to the plaintiff. It is declared that neither parties legal representatives are entitled to any fees or disbursements in respect of any work or service performed in respect of this matter.

V/O: We tried to contact Ketsekele’s lawyer Fransie van Niekerk at her offices in Brooklyn, but she refused to meet with us. We then went to her home in Kameelsdrift, but the intercom wasn’t working and the property was inaccessible.

Fransi: I think it’s improper to grant an interview at this stage as we’ve got instructions to appeal and as far as we are concerned this matter is sub judice.

V/O: The sub judice rule is regarded by many legal scholars as archaic, but is still raised as an excuse not to comment on matters that are already in the public domain.

Chris: I think an appeal is certainly not indicated. This was fraud. It was conscious, pernicious, deliberate fraud.

V/O: The President of the Law Society Strike Madiba was also scathing.

Strike: This is a very, very serious transgression. We as the Law Society take a very dim of what transpired. We have as of now started with our investigations, and then we will definitely refer it to our investigating team.

Nana: If the Bar Council feels that this person is not proper and fit to continue to practice as an advocate, then we will approach the Court for that person to be suspended or to be struck off the roll of advocates as the Court may deem it necessary.

John link: The abuse of the system has effectively drained the RAF’s coffers. That means that accident victims who have had successful claims often aren’t being paid their money, even when there’s a court order to that effect.

V/O: Like Alison Law had to wait 6 months before the RAF was finally able to pay her claim at the end of May.

Jonathan: The question in my mind is would there have been money if you don’t have instances such as the Bertelsmann case. All these experts talking about serious injury, and here I am dealing with a daughter who had serious injuries. That they would even contemplate trying to waste time and money on someone with a bent little finger – it’s just nauseating.

The RAF have run out of money, partly due to the fact that lawyers like those representing Welcome Ketsekele, routinely claim at least R300 000 in costs. This leaves legitimate benefactors like Alison Law out of pocket and struggling to survive.
